anchors.source_read: PDF (version of record, MMWR 72(35):949-956), all 8 pages; the Figure read on a 200-dpi rendering; Tables 1-2 and their footnotes in the text layer
anchors.extracted: Jurisdictions in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS) entered unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths from death certificates, post-mortem toxicology and medical examiner or coroner reports. Trends used the 30 jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia) with complete data for July 2019 to December 2021, and the 2021 characteristics 35 jurisdictions; four states (five in 2021) reported only from counties with at least 75% of their 2017 overdose deaths; analysis was restricted to deaths with a medical examiner or coroner report. Deaths were flagged by a counterfeit-pill checkbox or by text searches of the narrative (for example for 'counterf' or 'M-30', or for oxycodone or alprazolam brand names when that drug was absent on toxicology), and flagged narratives were coded by two coauthors. Evidence of counterfeit pill use was any of: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit by witnesses, police, medical examiners or coroners; pills testing positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; oxycodone- or alprazolam-looking pills with that drug absent on post-mortem toxicology; unmarked pills; or a witness report of pill use when none of the drugs detected exists in legitimate pill form. How many deaths met each criterion, or involved laboratory-tested pills, is not reported.

anchors.source_read: PDF (version of record, MMWR 72(35):949-956), all 8 pages; the Figure read on a 200-dpi rendering; Tables 1-2 and their footnotes in the text layer
anchors.extracted: The authors infer that, because counterfeit pills often contain illicitly manufactured fentanyls and only these were involved in many of the deaths, the pills used likely contained the drugs that caused death. Limitations they state: the results may not generalize beyond the included jurisdictions; documentation of counterfeit pill use relied on the completeness of medical examiner and coroner reports, is likely underestimated, and the underestimation likely varies within and between jurisdictions; and the definition included pills found or reported at the scene, so some deaths may be counted even if the person did not use the pills.

anchors.extracted: Staff of six overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City: Citiwide and Positive Health Project), approached at a national conference, were each asked to recruit five people trained and five not trained by their programme, at sites where people who use or used drugs gather; participants were paid $10 and completed a paper questionnaire on their own, with site staff available for questions or to administer it when literacy was a problem. 62 took part between October 2005 and July 2006: 30 trained (a median of 8 months before, range 1–80 months) and 32 untrained (three trained elsewhere, counted as untrained); 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff (needle-exchange employees were 30.0% of the trained and 15.6% of the untrained).

anchors.locator: Methods › Evaluation tool, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.source_read: PDF (online-first version of the Addiction article, paginated 1-11), all pages; Tables 1-4 in the text layer
anchors.extracted: The 16 scenarios were experiences that people who inject drugs had described as overdoses, chosen from 60 reported in a study of public injecting; development and validation are reported elsewhere (a 2006 conference abstract). Eleven medical experts classified each as opioid overdose, non-opioid overdose, not an overdose, or not enough information/unsure, and said whether naloxone was indicated; with the non-opioid and non-overdose categories collapsed, latent class analysis of their answers gave the key: 9 opioid overdoses, all requiring naloxone, and 7 non-opioid or non-overdose scenarios, not requiring it. Recognition and naloxone scores each ranged from 0 to 16. No data were gathered on age, race, ethnicity or drugs used. The scenario texts are not printed.

anchors.extracted: For each tablet, logo, diameter, thickness, weight, colour and groove were recorded; a tablet from a batch already analysed by GC-MS at least three times was taken as identified by its colour-test result and these features, and the person who brought it was given the batch's average content and range. The authors state that this recognition has proven very reliable in the Netherlands, citing earlier work, with no data in this paper, and do not say whether such tablets are counted in the figures. Limits they state: people using the services do not necessarily represent all people who use drugs; the services differed greatly in scale; an unknown proportion of people are not interested in testing; the laboratories used different techniques and sensitivities and reported purity as salt or base, which may have led to underreporting of new substances and adulterants.
